chunks.title: Baroque Chiaroscuro
chunks.content: Baroque chiaroscuro is the dramatic orchestration of light and shadow pioneered by Caravaggio in Rome around 1600 and developed across Europe by Rembrandt, Artemisia Gentileschi, Jusepe de Ribera, and Georges de La Tour. The convention treats light as a directed beam entering an otherwise dark interior, falling on selected figures or objects while the surrounding world falls into deep umber or near-black. The technique requires a value structure organized around a narrow mid-tone range and a single dominant light source, often positioned just outside the canvas so the beam is felt rather than seen. Caravaggio's tenebrism pushes this to extremes; Rembrandt's late work softens the beam with atmospheric diffusion and reintroduces lost edges in the shadows. Painters working in this convention typically begin with an imprimatura of burnt sienna or raw umber and build lights with opaque mixtures of lead white, Naples yellow, and warm earths. When prompting a reference generator for a chiaroscuro convention, name the single light source and the value range from deepest mass to highest light.

chunks.title: Renaissance Sfumato
chunks.content: Sfumato is the smoky, imperceptible transition between tones and colors developed by Leonardo da Vinci in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries and adopted by Correggio, Giorgione, and the early Titian. The word derives from the Italian sfumare, meaning to evaporate like smoke. Sfumato is achieved by glazing and scumbling thin, semi-transparent films of oil paint over a carefully modeled underpainting, allowing each successive layer to soften the transition beneath it. Unlike a hard edge, a sfumato edge has no single contour; the form passes gradually through a zone of intermediate values. The Mona Lisa is the paradigm: the corners of the mouth and eyes are not drawn but dissolved, so the expression is unstable and alive. The technique requires patience, since sfumato cannot be achieved alla prima because it depends on the slow drying of oil and the controlled layering of translucent films. Painters typically use lean paint with a touch of linseed or walnut medium. When prompting a reference generator for a sfumato convention, name the dissolved-edge zones and the glazing method.

chunks.title: Impressionist Broken Color
chunks.content: Impressionist broken color is the practice of placing small, distinct strokes of pure pigment side by side and allowing optical mixing in the viewer's eye rather than premixing on the palette. Pioneered by Monet, Renoir, Pissarro, and Sisley in the 1870s, the convention rejects the smooth, blended finish of academic painting in favor of a vibrating, high-chroma surface. Each stroke carries its own local color, value, and temperature, and adjacent strokes are often complements, so a blue stroke sits next to an orange stroke next to a violet stroke, and the eye reads the passage as a unified hue only at a distance. The technique depends on a relatively high-key value range, loose gestural brushwork, and pigments that retain their chroma when juxtaposed: cobalt blue, viridian, cadmium yellow, cadmium red, and the ceruleans. Earth pigments such as burnt sienna and yellow ochre are used as binders but rarely as the stars. When prompting a reference generator for an Impressionist broken-color convention, name the stroke type and the chroma priority.

chunks.title: Alla Prima Freshness
chunks.content: Alla-prima freshness describes the confident, single-session painting technique in which the entire picture is resolved in one sitting while the paint remains wet. Associated with John Singer Sargent, Joaquin Sorolla, Mary Cassatt, Anders Zorn, and Cecilia Beaux, the convention prizes directness, gestural economy, and the visible evidence of a thinking hand. Alla prima requires a prepared ground of correct value and approximate local color, often an imprimatura or a toned canvas, so the painter is laying relationships rather than searching for them. The brushwork is loaded, the marks are committed, and there is little reworking. The convention depends on the fat-over-lean rule to avoid cracking: lean mixtures go down first, fatter mixtures on top. The hallmark of an alla prima picture is the freshness of the edges — crisp where decisive, lost where the artist changed their mind, and never overworked. Palette-knife ridges, gestural streaks radiating outward, and scraped dragged smeared paint are all signatures. When prompting a reference generator for alla-prima freshness, name the single-session commitment and the gestural stroke vocabulary.

chunks.title: Northern Realism
chunks.content: Northern realism describes the meticulous, observational tradition associated with Vermeer, Holbein, van Eyck, and the seventeenth-century Dutch and Flemish masters. The convention prizes faithful description of surface, light, and material, achieved through patient layering and the use of magnifying optics or camera obscura aids. Vermeer's pearly interiors are rendered with tiny, almost invisible strokes of lead white over a cool imprimatura; each plane is built up through successive glazes until the surface glows with internal light. Holbein's portraits depend on linear precision and the disciplined restraint of palette; van Eyck's oil technique pioneered the medium itself. The convention requires slow drying times and is incompatible with alla prima. Pigments are typically the transparent earths and lakes: madder, indigo, bone black, raw umber, and the lead-tin yellows. The hallmark of Northern realism is the legibility of material: light on a brass nail reads differently from light on a satin sleeve. When prompting a reference generator, name the material surfaces and the layered glazing commitment.

chunks.title: Fauvism
chunks.content: Fauvism, the early-twentieth-century movement led by Henri Matisse, Andre Derain, and Maurice de Vlaminck, liberated color from descriptive function and elevated it to the primary expressive element. Fauvist canvases use pure, saturated pigment straight from the tube — cadmium red, viridian, cobalt blue, chrome yellow — and reject naturalistic local color in favor of emotional and structural intent. A Fauvist landscape might use vermillion for grass, cobalt for shadows, and cadmium yellow for sky. The convention depends on a flat, decorative application: the brushstroke is broad and unmodulated, the paint is often applied with palette knife or stiff bristle, and the surface preserves the gesture of the mark. Despite the chromatic freedom, Fauvist compositions are rigorously structured; Matisse was a master of pattern and balance. The convention is incompatible with smooth academic finish; the visible brushstroke is essential. When prompting a reference generator for a Fauvist convention, name the non-natural color assignments and the broad flat brushwork.

chunks.title: Expressionist Gestural Brushwork
chunks.content: Expressionist gestural brushwork, associated with Chaim Soutine, Frank Auerbach, Leon Kossoff, and the broader twentieth-century expressionist tradition, treats the brushstroke as a record of the painter's emotional and physical engagement with the surface. The convention rejects smooth finish in favor of impasto built up over many sessions, with each layer preserving the evidence of the previous stroke. Soutine's carcasses and trees are scraped, dragged, smeared, and reworked until the paint surface is a palimpsest of intentions. Auerbach's London streets are built up in thick, scumbled layers of earth pigment until the impasto stands in relief from the canvas. The convention requires oil paint of stiff consistency and brushes that can push, scrape, and load heavily. The hallmark of expressionist gestural brushwork is the autonomy of the stroke: each mark is a self-contained event that contributes to the overall picture without being subordinated to a polished surface. When prompting a reference generator, name the impasto build-up and the gestural stroke vocabulary.

chunks.title: Rococo Pastel Palette
chunks.content: Rococo pastel palette describes the high-key, lightly saturated color scheme associated with Antoine Watteau, Jean-Honore Fragonard, Francois Boucher, and the eighteenth-century French court painters. The convention favors a luminous, airy atmosphere built from soft blues, dusty roses, creamy yellows, sage greens, and pearl grays, with the deepest shadows rarely descending below middle-value. Pigments are typically the chalky, opaque earths and the cooler synthetic pigments: cerulean blue, Naples yellow, terra rosa, and the lake-based pinks. Brushwork is light, feathery, and often applied in thin broken strokes that allow the ground to show through. The convention depends on a luminous imprimatura — typically a warm gray or pale terra rosa — and on restraint in the shadows. Rococo subjects are typically intimate, decorative, and pastoral; the palette supports rather than competes with the subject. When prompting a reference generator for a Rococo pastel palette, name the high-key value range and the named pigment vocabulary.

chunks.title: Classical Contrapposto and Balance
chunks.content: Classical contrapposto and balance, codified by the High Renaissance — Raphael, Michelangelo, and Ingres — describes the figurative convention in which the body's weight rests on one leg while the other is relaxed, producing an asymmetric S-curve through the torso. The pose creates a tension between stability and movement that classical theorists considered the foundation of dignified figure composition. The convention is not limited to figures: classical balance extends to still life, where the visual weight on one side of a vertical axis is matched by a different kind of weight on the other, and to landscape, where a heavy mass on one side is answered by an open sky or a smaller accent on the other. The principle is balance, not symmetry. Ingres's portraits are rigorously balanced — the figure's weight rests on one leg, the head tilts to oppose, the gaze leads the eye through a controlled path. The convention depends on a clear value hierarchy and a careful drawing stage before any color is applied. When prompting a reference generator for classical balance, name the dominant axis and the weight distribution.
